pages.text: $(bold)Ore in Materialism$(0)$(br2)Forget the steady scatter of ordinary TerraFirmaCraft. Here, veins are $(thing)far larger$(0) — a single deposit can be an enormous haul — but also $(thing)much rarer$(0), set well apart across the world.$(br2)The trade is deliberate: you will find fewer veins, but each one is a serious reward worth mining out in full.

Rarer ore would be a cruel thing if it were also $(italic)hidden$(0) — but it is not. Almost every deposit announces itself with a $(thing)surface indicator$(0): small loose samples of its ore lying on the ground directly above the vein.$(br2)So prospecting here is less about luck and more about $(thing)reading the ground$(0). Cover distance, watch for those tell-tale samples, and you will rarely walk past a vein without knowing it.

Where an ore can appear depends on the $(thing)rock$(0) around it. Rocks come in four families: $(thing)igneous extrusive$(0) (rhyolite, basalt, andesite, dacite), $(thing)igneous intrusive$(0) (granite, diorite, gabbro), $(thing)sedimentary$(0) (limestone, shale, chert, dolomite and more), and $(thing)metamorphic$(0) (marble, slate, gneiss, schist, quartzite, phyllite).

Each entry in this category lists, for an ore: the $(thing)rock types$(0) that host it, the $(thing)Y-range$(0) to search, its relative $(thing)rarity$(0), and whether it leaves a surface sample.$(br2)Remember that a region holds only a few rock types, so some ores simply will not exist where you stand — if the right stone is not here, you must travel to find it.
